title: OKLCH — The Modern Colour Space for Design Systems
content: OKLCH (OK Lightness Chroma Hue) is the modern perceptually-uniform colour space, succeeding HSL and LCH for design system use. Built on the Oklab colour model by Björn Ottosson (2020). Three axes: L (Lightness) — 0=black, 1=white, perceptually linear, meaning L:0.5 looks equally bright regardless of hue. C (Chroma) — 0=grey, 0.4=vivid, represents colourfulness. H (Hue) — 0-360° colour wheel. CSS Color 4 syntax: oklch(0.55 0.18 250). Why it matters for design systems: (1) Perceptually uniform lightness — you can build a colour scale where every step feels equally different, which is impossible with HSL. (2) Predictable chroma — colours at the same C value look equally vivid. (3) Wide-gamut support — OKLCH can represent P3 and Rec2020 colours that HSL cannot. (4) Hue consistency — blending between two OKLCH colours doesn't create unexpected hue shifts (HSL interpolation can produce ugly intermediate hues). Browser support: Chrome 111+, Safari 15.4+, Firefox 113+. Figma: OKLCH available in the colour picker since 2024. Tools: oklch.com (interactive picker by Andrey Sitnik), culori.js (JavaScript colour library), Radix UI Colours (built with OKLCH).

title: OKLCH vs HSL — Why the Difference Matters
content: The core problem with HSL for design systems: HSL lightness is not perceptually uniform. Yellow at L:50% looks dramatically brighter than blue at L:50% because the human eye is far more sensitive to yellow-green light. This creates colour scales that feel unbalanced — yellows appear to 'jump out' of a palette while blues look dim at the same HSL lightness. OKLCH lightness is derived from human vision research (CIECAM16-based) and is perceptually calibrated — colours at the same L value truly appear equally bright. Practical impact: (1) A 10-shade neutral scale built in HSL will have uneven perceived steps — some transitions look larger than others. Built in OKLCH, each step feels equal. (2) Semantic colours (success green, warning yellow, error red, info blue) built at the same OKLCH L value naturally harmonize as a group — they all feel the same 'weight'. In HSL, yellow and red at the same L:50% look wildly different. (3) Dark mode remapping is more predictable in OKLCH — flipping L from 0.3 to 0.7 gives a true visual inversion rather than HSL's approximation. RECOMMENDATION: build all primitive colour palettes in OKLCH, export to hex for broad tool compatibility where needed, but store the OKLCH source values as the canonical representation.

title: Building Colour Scales with OKLCH — Step by Step
content: Building a 10-step colour scale in OKLCH. Step 1: Choose the hue (H). Example: blue = H:250. Fix this value for all 10 shades. Step 2: Choose a chroma (C) value. Vivid: C:0.20-0.25. Muted/neutral: C:0.03-0.08. Brand-intensity: C:0.15-0.18. Keep C consistent across shades to maintain equal saturation. Step 3: Define 10 lightness values spread evenly from L:0.96 (shade 50) to L:0.18 (shade 950). Example scale: 50=0.96, 100=0.90, 200=0.82, 300=0.72, 400=0.62, 500=0.55, 600=0.46, 700=0.36, 800=0.26, 900=0.18. The 0.10 steps feel perceptually even in OKLCH. Step 4: Check that shade 500 passes WCAG 3:1 against white (it often won't — adjust C or L until contrast is adequate). Step 5: Verify chroma doesn't exceed the sRGB gamut at light shades — reduce C for shades 50-200 if colours look washed out. OKLCH gamut tip: oklch.com shows which values fall outside sRGB gamut in red — stay inside for maximum compatibility. SHORTCUT: use Radix UI colour palette generator or the oklch.com palette tool which automates steps 2-5.

title: OKLCH in Figma and CSS — Practical Usage
content: USING OKLCH IN FIGMA: Figma's colour picker includes OKLCH mode as of 2024. To access: open the colour picker, click the hex/colour mode dropdown, select OKLCH. Values display as L (0-1), C (0-0.4+), H (0-360). You can enter OKLCH values directly. Variable values can be set in OKLCH mode — Figma stores the colour internally and converts to sRGB for the canvas. IMPORTANT: Figma still renders in sRGB on the canvas. OKLCH values outside the sRGB gamut are clamped — the canvas shows the clamped version. Use the P3 colour profile (View > Color Profile) if your devices support P3 gamut. OKLCH IN CSS (Color 4): oklch(0.55 0.18 250) — directly in CSS. With alpha: oklch(0.55 0.18 250 / 0.8). CSS variable: --color-primary: oklch(0.55 0.18 250). Browser fallback for older browsers: provide the hex equivalent before the OKLCH value: background: #2563eb; background: oklch(0.55 0.18 250). HANDOFF RECOMMENDATION: store OKLCH as the canonical source in design tokens (DTCG format). Export to hex for backward compatibility. When developers use CSS Color 4, the OKLCH values are directly usable. OKLCH colour tokens enable colour manipulation in CSS (calc() on L channel for hover states) without JavaScript.

meta.css: oklch(L C H) or oklch(L C H / alpha)

title: Dark Mode Strategies — Dark Elevated vs Dark Deep
content: Two distinct philosophies for building dark mode surface colours. DARK ELEVATED strategy: maintains the same lightness progression direction as light mode. In light mode, surfaces get darker as elevation increases (background < card < modal). In dark mode, surfaces also get lighter as elevation increases (dark-bg=L:0.12, dark-card=L:0.16, dark-modal=L:0.20). This mirrors the light mode logic and is the approach used by Material Design 3. Advantage: intuitive and predictable — same mental model in both modes. Disadvantage: all dark surfaces look similar without strong contrast. DARK DEEP strategy: reverses the direction in dark mode. The base is the darkest, and the top of the stack (deepest-elevated, like a modal backdrop) uses the darker values, while interactive surfaces use slightly lighter values to stand out. Advantage: creates a 'night sky' feeling where depth goes deeper rather than lighter. Works well for media apps, gaming, creative tools. CHOOSING: use Dark Elevated for productivity, enterprise, and cross-platform products (matches iOS/Android conventions). Use Dark Deep for immersive experiences, creative tools, and entertainment products. IMPLEMENTATION: in both strategies, define 4-6 surface levels as semantic tokens (surface-1 through surface-5) and remap them in the Dark mode.

title: Linear Progression Palette — 48-Step Neutral Scale
content: A high-resolution neutral scale provides fine-grained control for elevation and state surfaces. The 48-step model uses consistent 2% lightness increments from 0% to 96% (48 steps × 2% = 96%). CONSTRUCTION: fix a single hue and chroma across all 48 steps. Example: H:220 (cool blue-grey), C:0.025 (very low saturation). Steps: 00=L:0.98 (near white), 02=L:0.96, 04=L:0.94, ..., 96=L:0.02 (near black). NAME by lightness percentage: neutral-00, neutral-02, neutral-04, etc. This naming directly communicates the lightness value. ADVANTAGE: precise control over small distinctions — elevation differences of 2 lightness steps are visible and intentional. More steps means fewer compromises when mapping semantics. PRACTICAL SUBSET: expose only a subset as semantic tokens (don't expose all 48 to designers) — use the full palette as primitives and map semantic tokens (surface-1=neutral-96, surface-2=neutral-94, border-subtle=neutral-90) to the appropriate steps. DARK MODE: map semantic tokens to higher-numbered steps (darker) in dark mode: surface-1=neutral-10, surface-2=neutral-12, border-subtle=neutral-20. SINGLE HUE RULE: using one hue across all neutrals gives the scale a consistent temperature — cool-tinted greys feel professional and modern, warm-tinted greys feel approachable and editorial.

title: Accent Palette Architecture — 16 Colours × 9 Shades
content: A robust accent colour system: 16 hues × 9 shades = 144 primitive colour tokens. Hues cover the full spectrum: red, orange, amber, yellow, lime, green, teal, cyan, sky, blue, indigo, violet, purple, fuchsia, pink, rose. 9 shades per hue: 100 (lightest tint), 200, 300, 400 (base for non-text), 500 (base for text on dark), 600 (primary interactive, passes WCAG on white), 700 (hover state), 800, 900 (darkest). SHADE CONTRAST CONVENTIONS: Shade 600 and 500 — distinct enough for borders and decorative elements. Shade 300 — primary colour for interactive elements (buttons, links, checked states). Shade 400 — for non-text elements that need less contrast (icons in data visualisation, chart elements). Shades 200 and 100 — tints and highlights (chip backgrounds, tag backgrounds, subtle banners). SEMANTIC MAPPING: each semantic colour category (action, success, warning, danger, info) maps to one of these hue families. action → blue-300, success → green-300, warning → amber-300, danger → red-300. The full 16-colour palette gives future flexibility — you can introduce new semantic categories without adding new primitives. WHY 16: provides enough variety for distinct, non-confusable semantic colours while remaining a manageable set.

title: Shade Contrast Rules — Which Shade for Which Purpose
content: Consistent shade-to-purpose mapping creates predictable accessibility. RULE BY SHADE: Shade 50/100 — tint backgrounds, subtle chip fills, hover overlays on white. Passes no contrast requirement — purely decorative. Shade 200/300 — tinted surfaces for selected states, active indicators, chart fills. Shade 400 — non-text elements: icons in charts, data visualisation marks, decorative dividers. Meets WCAG 3:1 for UI components (non-text contrast). Shade 500 — border colours on white in light mode. Passes 3:1 UI component contrast. Primary colour in dark mode on dark surfaces. Shade 600 — primary interactive colour on white backgrounds. Passes WCAG AA 4.5:1 for text. Use for links, button backgrounds, active states. Shade 700 — hover state for shade 600 interactive elements. Shade 800/900 — text on coloured backgrounds (e.g., text inside a coloured badge). INDEPENDENT TEXT COLOUR: do not use accent shades for body text on white — use the neutral scale. An independent text colour palette (neutral-900 for primary text, neutral-600 for secondary) ensures WCAG compliance without depending on accent shade math. VERIFICATION: check every shade/background combination with a contrast calculator before assigning it a semantic role.

title: 60-30-10 Rule Applied to Design System Tokens
content: The 60-30-10 colour cadence principle applied to design token architecture. 60% — DOMINANT (Surface tokens): neutral background and surface colours. surface/page, surface/default, surface/subtle, surface/muted. These should be near-white (light) or dark grey (dark). This is the bulk of the visual field — walls, cards, containers. 30% — SECONDARY (Content tokens): text colours, icon colours, and secondary UI elements. text/primary, text/secondary, text/tertiary, icon/default, border/default. These define the content layer that sits on the 60% surfaces. 10% — ACCENT (Action tokens): brand primary colour, interactive elements, CTAs, links, selected states. action/primary, color/link, color/selected. This should appear sparingly — only on elements that need to draw attention. APPLICATION IN FIGMA: when building a new screen, start with surface tokens (the 60), add text and border tokens (the 30), and only apply action tokens to the elements that need to direct user behaviour (the 10). DARK MODE: the cadence is preserved — surfaces become dark greys, content tokens become light greys, accent tokens stay vivid but may shift chroma slightly. COMMON MISTAKE: making the brand colour 60% of the screen creates a visually exhausting interface that dilutes the brand instead of strengthening it. The accent is powerful precisely because it is rare.

title: Utility Colours — Opacity and Theme-Dependent Values
content: Utility colours are semi-transparent values that adapt to the background they sit on. Two categories: OVERLAY utilities — darken or lighten the surface beneath. Used for hover states, pressed states, modal backdrops. Examples: overlay/hover (black at 5% opacity for light mode, white at 8% opacity for dark mode), overlay/pressed (black at 10% / white at 12%), overlay/backdrop (black at 50%). These are theme-dependent — the overlay colour changes between light and dark mode to create the right contrast effect. TINT utilities — add a coloured wash over content. Used for highlighted rows, selected items, banners. Examples: tint/primary (action-primary at 8-10% opacity), tint/success (success colour at 10%), tint/danger (danger colour at 8%). IMPLEMENTATION IN FIGMA: create colour variables with opacity embedded using the alpha channel of the colour. Set up Light and Dark modes — in Light mode the overlay is black-semi-transparent, in Dark mode it is white-semi-transparent. This way designers get automatic theming for all overlay states. RULE: utility colours must always reference neutral colours (black/white or the primary hue) rather than specific primitive colours. A blue-at-10% hover state is a tint utility, not a primitive usage.
